How Bihar's land survey is reshaping rural disputes

Two years into Bihar's ambitious revisional land survey, the first large-scale evidence of its effects is emerging from the state's clogged land tribunals.

Data compiled from six districts shows mutation disputes pending for over a year have fallen by nearly a third since survey teams began publishing draft records.

Revenue officials attribute the decline to the survey's ground-truthing process, which forces rival claimants to produce documents before village-level functionaries.

But lawyers caution that the survey has also surfaced dormant conflicts, particularly where inheritance was never partitioned across generations.

Land rights researchers argue the real test will come at the claims-and-objections stage, when draft maps are thrown open to challenge.

The survey, covering over 45,000 villages, is scheduled for completion next year, though officials privately concede difficult terrain may spill over.

For now, the numbers suggest a slow but measurable shift from possession-based claims to record-based ownership.

Whether that shift survives the appellate courts will decide the survey's legacy, experts say.

Notes: data from tribunal records; interviews with officials.
